content.thinking:
I'm checking the root-cause claim: request volume to io-shop has risen well above its earlier level, but the service still runs on three replicas with a fixed CPU limit. That means CPU is pinned at the cap, so requests queue for CPU and latency climbs. I want to confirm the 3.0-core limit against the config before I accept it.

I'm going through the list of claims one by one, checking each against the records. The cause-in-plain-words line and the symptom line both hold up against the evidence, and the causal-chain points about latency and CPU sitting at the limit also check out.

I'm checking the replica count against the record: at the onset it was still three, with nothing showing autoscaling, and I'm reading the "by hand" scale-out as the Mitigation Agent's manual change. I'm also treating the code-fix attribution as hedged, which fits the evidence so far, and I'm noting that nobody was paged.

content.text:
I found no claims to flag. Every factual claim in the document is backed by the record, and the hedged or attributed ones are worded as the record allows.

- **Cause:** The load-against-CPU root cause and causal-chain links 2–4 are backed by R1 (requests 1200/min rising to a 5400/min peak), R2 (CPU at 94% of its limit on average, 100% at peak) and T7 (3 replicas). The record's own line says the load, not the service, is what changed.
- **"Nothing about the service changed":** T9 (no production changes read back) and T12 (no flag changes) back this.
- **Contributing factor 1 (no replicas added):** T7 and T19 show the service at 3 replicas until the Mitigation Agent scaled it out, and AI-3 calls that a change Argus made "by hand". Nothing in the record shows autoscaling.
- **Contributing factor 2 (the account-page code):** It is credited to Code-Fix and hedged ("likely", "Nothing ran this reading"), as F1 requires.
- **Not judged:** I didn't check the "had it been otherwise" fields (only their what-ifs, which aren't judged), the action items, or the went-well/went-wrong verdict itself. I did check the fact in "went wrong" that nobody was paged, and it is supported.

supported.quote: Request volume to io-shop rose well above its earlier level while the service ran on a fixed amount of CPU ({T7.2} replicas, each under a CPU limit, as of T7). CPU use climbed to that limit, so requests had to wait for CPU and response times stretched.
rows: The record confirmed [C1]: the load outgrew the CPU the service had

supported.quote: Far more requests than usual reached the shop and used up the fixed amount of computing power its servers had, so requests had to wait their turn; the shop's account page likely also does much more work per request than it needs to, which made that limit come sooner.
rows: The record confirmed [C1]: the load outgrew the CPU the service had

supported.quote: Another rise in request volume could use up the service's CPU again and slow its responses the same way.
rows: The record confirmed [C1]: the load outgrew the CPU the service had
The series behind the alert ... 214.76666666666668 ms before it began, 1316.5 ms on average while it was broken

supported.quote: People using the shop waited much longer for responses: from the onset, the response time that nearly all requests stay under climbed far above its usual level, and the latency alert fired.
rows: The series behind the alert ... 214.76666666666668 ms before it began, 1316.5 ms on average while it was broken, and 1803 ms at its worst

supported.quote: Requests were waiting for CPU: the service's CPU use rose to the limit set for it and stayed close to that limit while the service was broken.
The CPU filled up because request volume climbed far above its earlier level. Nothing about the service changed: the change that set the incident off was the rise in load.
rows: What changed before it began was the load, not the service

supported.quote: The higher volume outgrew the fixed CPU that the service's {T7.2} replicas had as of T7.
The service did not add replicas as load grew. It stayed at {T7.2} replicas (as of T7) until the Mitigation Agent scaled it out by hand. No autoscaling of io-shop was seen in the record.

According to Code-Fix's reading of src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, on the account page's default path (when neither rollout flag is set), each render likely re-adds every purchase up to each one in turn, a growing prefix of the shopper's history, where a single pass would give the same number. That would make each request cost far more CPU than its answer needs. Nothing ran this reading.
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to the alert, so no person was brought in when it fired.
rows: Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one.
